title: One-way permutations from one-way functions
formal: Does the existence of classical one-way functions secure against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries imply the existence of a classical, efficiently generated family of full-domain one-way permutations with the same security convention?
definitions: A one-way function is a uniformly polynomial-time computable family f_n:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1}^{ℓ(n)}, for a polynomially bounded, computable output length ℓ, such that for every randomized polynomial-size circuit family A_n, Pr[f_n(A_n(1ⁿ,f_n(X)))=f_n(X)] is negligible in n for uniform X∈{0,1}ⁿ; outputs outside {0,1}ⁿ fail. A function μ is negligible if for every c>0, μ(n)≤n^{-c} for all sufficiently large n. A permutation family consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time key generator Gen(1ⁿ) and deterministic polynomial-time evaluation Eval(1ⁿ,pk,x), with a fixed polynomially bounded, polynomial-time computable integer m(n)≥n. For every pk in the support of Gen(1ⁿ), Eval defines a bijection π_pk:{0,1}^{m(n)}→{0,1}^{m(n)}. For every randomized polynomial-size adversary A_n, Pr[π_pk(A_n(1ⁿ,pk,π_pk(X)))=π_pk(X)] must be negligible, with pk←Gen(1ⁿ), independent uniform X and independent adversary coins. Malformed outputs fail. The public key is available to the attacker; no trapdoor is required or given. All security is classical. “Full-domain” fixes the input set to the whole Boolean cube; the valid public-key set need not be all bit strings of its length. The implication is an ordinary existence implication, without restrictions to black-box constructions and without extra assumptions such as obfuscation or subexponential security.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence implication, allowing any mathematical construction or proof technique, or refute that implication in the ordinary computational model. Proving that one-way functions do not exist would make the implication vacuously true. An oracle separation or a theorem excluding a restricted class of reductions is a construction barrier, not a refutation of the unrestricted implication. A permutation family on special sparse domains does not meet the full-domain convention fixed here; an additional trapdoor property would be a stronger positive result.
context:
A one-way function is easy to evaluate but hard to invert on a random input. It may identify many different inputs and need not cover its output space. A one-way permutation has exactly one preimage for every output in its domain. The extra requirement is structural: nothing is lost mathematically, yet efficiently recovering the uniquely determined input must remain infeasible.

This card fixes the full-domain, public-key family version because the original phrase “one-way permutation” leaves several conventions unspecified. A public key chooses a permutation of an entire Boolean cube; all input strings of that length are valid. A stronger unkeyed formulation asks for a single length-preserving permutation on all bit strings. A more permissive formulation allows key-dependent sparse domains. Results in those settings must be compared with their domain and sampling requirements visible.

Making a computation reversible is not enough. The map (x,z)↦(x,z XOR f(x)) is a bijection for any efficiently computable length-compatible f, but its inverse is obtained by applying exactly the same map. Likewise, simply attaching x to f(x) makes the output injective while revealing the desired preimage. The construction has to preserve computational difficulty while removing collisions and covering the domain, without publishing the information needed for inversion.

Many other forms of cryptographic structure can be derived from bare one-wayness. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby show that every one-way function yields a pseudorandom generator. That success does not enforce bijectivity. The permutation question tests whether computational hardness can always be reorganized into a particularly rigid, uniquely invertible mathematical object.

Rudich’s 1988 thesis developed the oracle-separation approach and gave a barrier for this implication conditional on a combinatorial conjecture. The thesis abstract states that qualification explicitly. It is misleading to describe the original thesis alone as an unconditional separation of the ordinary existence assumptions. An oracle world changes what algorithms can access, so it diagnoses limitations of proof techniques rather than settling the actual implication.

Matsuda and Matsuura subsequently prove a fully black-box barrier even when the starting function is injective, increases length by only one bit, and satisfies their stronger adaptive one-wayness condition. Thus an apparently tiny departure from a permutation already defeats a broad class of generic constructions. Their result concerns constructions that treat the supplied primitive and adversary through specified interfaces; it does not exclude exploiting the code or other structure of a concrete function.

Asharov and Segev address another subtlety: earlier negative arguments could fail when the construction’s domains depended on the underlying primitives. They exclude black-box constructions from one-way functions even without that domain-invariance requirement. They also give a separate barrier for constructions using oracle-aided indistinguishability obfuscation, under domain-invariance conditions. The two statements have different assumptions and should not be merged into an unrestricted impossibility theorem.

There is significant progress with stronger assumptions. Shmueli and Zhandry’s July 2025 paper constructs full-domain trapdoor one-way permutations assuming subexponentially secure indistinguishability obfuscation and subexponentially secure one-way functions. It uses a new kind of pseudorandom permutation that supports controlled permutation of its outputs. The trapdoor guarantee is stronger than this card requests, but both the extra primitive and the stronger hardness assumptions prevent this from proving the target implication.

The same paper explains why its full-domain result is compatible with the earlier obfuscation barrier. Its input domain is the whole cube, but its public keys are obfuscated programs. The valid-key domain therefore depends on the building blocks. The older formal domain-invariance condition constrains both input and key domains. Keeping these two notions separate prevents an erroneous claim that a published barrier has been contradicted.

A positive answer would show that unique, length-preserving inversion hardness is available whenever basic cryptographic hardness exists. A negative answer would reveal a structural separation inside foundational cryptographic assumptions. Existing barriers make the problem especially informative: a successful construction from ordinary one-way functions would need to escape the established generic approaches, rather than merely improve their efficiency.
why: Determine whether basic average-case inversion hardness necessarily supports efficient bijections, a rigid primitive at the foundation of cryptographic constructions.

importance.reason: A longstanding question about the structure obtainable from minimal cryptographic assumptions, with strong construction barriers and a recent full-domain breakthrough under additional assumptions.

progress.text: Rudich develops oracle barriers; the thesis’s one-way-function-to-permutation argument is conditional on a combinatorial conjecture.
Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby establish pseudorandom generators from arbitrary one-way functions, without obtaining a permutation guarantee.
Matsuda–Matsuura exclude fully black-box constructions from even one-bit-expanding injective one-way functions with adaptive one-wayness.
Asharov–Segev handle domains depending on the primitives in their OWF-only barrier, and separately study domain-invariant constructions using obfuscation.
Shmueli–Zhandry obtain full-domain trapdoor permutations from subexponentially secure iO and OWFs; Section 1.4 distinguishes input-domain from key-domain invariance.

status_note: No derivation from ordinary one-way functions alone, or refutation of the unrestricted existence implication, was found through 11 September 2026. The 2025 full-domain trapdoor construction requires subexponential iO and OWF assumptions. Existing oracle and black-box barriers do not settle the unrestricted question. This card explicitly fixes the full-domain keyed convention.
